cards.front: What is the difference between an agonist and an antagonist at a receptor?
cards.back: An agonist binds the receptor and switches it on. An antagonist binds the same receptor, does nothing there, and keeps the agonist out.
cards.quote: An agonist binds a receptor and switches it on.
cards.section: A drug acts at a site it has to occupy

cards.front: Some receptors are partly active with nothing bound, and blockers that turn that background activity down are called {{c1::inverse agonists}}.
cards.quote: Some receptors are partly active with nothing bound, and some blockers, called inverse agonists, turn that background activity down.
cards.section: A drug acts at a site it has to occupy

cards.front: Nicotine made skeletal muscle contract and curare prevented it, even after the nerve to the muscle had been cut and had degenerated. What does that show?
cards.back: The drugs act on the muscle itself, not on the nerve. Langley called the site they act on the receptive substance.
cards.quote: and both still worked after the nerve to the muscle had been cut and had degenerated
cards.section: A drug acts at a site it has to occupy

cards.front: In the equilibrium, single-receptor model, for one agonist acting on one unchanged receptor population in one tissue, what does the response depend on?
cards.back: It is treated as a monotonic function of the fraction of receptors that agonist occupies. Binding sets that fraction (Kd is the only drug number in it); the agonist's efficacy and the tissue's amplifier turn it into a response that rises and saturates.
cards.quote: For one agonist acting on one unchanged receptor population in one tissue, the response is treated as a monotonic function of the fraction of receptors that agonist occupies.
cards.section: A drug acts at a site it has to occupy

cards.front: At equilibrium, fractional occupancy of a receptor = {{c1::[L] / (Kd + [L])}}, where [L] is the free ligand concentration.
cards.quote: occupancy = 1 / (Kd/[L] + 1) = [L] / (Kd + [L])

cards.front: The dissociation constant for L + R ⇌ LR is Kd = {{c1::k_off / k_on}}, which also equals [L][R]/[LR].
cards.quote: The ratio of the rate constants is the dissociation constant, Kd = k off /k on , which also equals [L][R]/[LR].

cards.front: What does Kd mean as a concentration, and what does a small Kd tell you?
cards.back: Kd is the free ligand concentration that half-fills the receptors. A small Kd means a tight grip: high affinity.
cards.quote: So Kd, the free ligand concentration that half-fills the receptors, measures affinity: a small Kd means a tight grip.

cards.front: A ligand binds its receptor with Kd = 4 nM. What free concentrations give 10% and 90% occupancy, and how many fold apart are they?
cards.back: 90% needs [L] = 9 × Kd = 36 nM; 10% needs [L] = Kd/9 ≈ 0.44 nM. They are 81-fold apart, nearly two powers of ten.

cards.front: Why are binding and dose–response curves drawn with concentration on a logarithmic axis?
cards.back: Going from 10% to 90% occupancy takes an 81-fold rise in ligand. On a linear axis the low-dose end is crushed against the origin; on a log axis the hyperbola becomes a symmetric S-shaped curve centred on Kd.
cards.quote: On a log axis the hyperbola becomes a symmetric S-shaped curve with Kd at its midpoint.

cards.front: The occupancy curve has the same hyperbolic form as the Michaelis–Menten equation. Why, and how do Kd and Km differ?
cards.back: Both describe a fixed number of sites being filled. Km combines several rate constants, while Kd is a pure binding constant.
cards.quote: One caution: Km combines several rate constants, while Kd is a pure binding constant.

cards.front: A radioligand binding curve rises from 10% to 90% of its maximum over only a 9-fold range of free ligand. What does that tell you about the binding sites?
cards.back: The sites are not acting independently: the binding is cooperative.
cards.why: Independent sites following [L]/(Kd + [L]) need an 81-fold rise to go from 10% to 90%.
cards.quote: A binding curve that climbs from 10% to 90% in much less than 81-fold means the sites are not acting independently.

cards.front: A tissue's dose–response curve rises from 10% to 90% of maximum over a 9-fold range of agonist. A student concludes the receptor binds the agonist cooperatively. Evaluate the claim and say what measurement would test it.
cards.back: Not justified. Steps after the receptor can steepen a response curve. Measure the binding curve itself (specific radioligand binding): a rise from 10% to 90% over much less than an 81-fold range of ligand points to cooperativity.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the 81-fold test applies to binding curves, not response curves.
cards.quote: steps after the receptor can steepen a response curve, so a steep one says nothing about receptor cooperativity by itself

cards.front: In a radioligand assay on greasy brain tissue, why must binding be saturable before you call it receptor binding?
cards.back: A finite set of sites fills up along the occupancy curve and levels off. Sticking to grease keeps rising with concentration.
cards.quote: A finite set of sites fills up along the occupancy curve, while sticking to grease keeps rising with concentration.

cards.front: How do you separate specific from nonspecific binding of a radioligand?
cards.back: Measure total binding, then measure again with a large excess of unlabelled drug, which keeps the label off the specific sites. Total minus nonspecific is specific binding, the curve that saturates.
cards.quote: Total minus nonspecific is specific binding, the curve that saturates.

cards.front: Levorphanol, an active opiate, displaced radioactive naloxone from brain membranes; dextrorphan, its mirror image with almost no opiate action, was far weaker. What does this show?
cards.back: The binding is stereospecific, so the label sits in a shaped pocket (a receptor), not in nonspecific grease.
cards.quote: Grease cannot tell a molecule from its mirror image.

cards.front: A saturation binding curve gives a Kd and the total count of sites, called {{c1::Bmax}}.
cards.quote: The saturation curve hands you the numbers in the occupancy equation, measured on the site itself: a Kd, and the total count of sites, called Bmax.

cards.front: At 6 nM radioligand, total binding is 900 fmol/mg protein and binding in excess unlabelled drug is 300 fmol/mg. Bmax for the specific sites is 800 fmol/mg. Estimate Kd.
cards.back: Specific binding = 900 − 300 = 600 fmol/mg, so occupancy = 600/800 = 0.75. [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 0.75 gives [L] = 3 × Kd, so Kd = 2 nM.
cards.quote: To see the saturable part, measure total binding, then measure it again with a large excess of unlabelled drug

cards.front: What is EC50, and what property of a drug does it measure?
cards.back: The concentration that gives half of the drug's maximum response. It measures potency: the lower the EC50, the less drug you need.
cards.quote: EC50 is the concentration that gives half of the drug's maximum response; it measures potency: the lower the EC50, the less drug you need.

cards.front: On a dose–response curve, {{c1::Emax}} is the largest response the drug can produce, however much you add.
cards.quote: Emax is the largest response the drug can produce, however much you add.

cards.front: Why can one agonist have a different EC50 in two tissues that carry the same receptor?
cards.back: EC50 mixes four quantities: the drug's affinity (Kd) and efficacy, and the tissue's receptor number and amplifier. The last two differ between tissues.
cards.quote: EC50 mixes all four, which is why one agonist's potency can differ between tissues.

cards.front: What distinguishes a partial agonist from a full agonist?
cards.back: A full agonist can drive the tissue to its maximum. A partial agonist levels off below it even when it occupies every receptor.
cards.quote: A partial agonist levels off below it even when it occupies every receptor

cards.front: In one tissue, drug A has EC50 = 5 nM and reaches 100% of the tissue maximum; drug B, at the same receptor, has EC50 = 0.5 nM and tops out at 50%. Compare potency and efficacy.
cards.back: B is 10-fold more potent (lower EC50). A has the greater efficacy (higher maximum); B is a partial agonist here.
cards.why: Potency is read from EC50; efficacy from Emax, below the tissue's ceiling.
cards.quote: a drug with an EC50 of 1 nM that tops out at 40% is as potent, and less efficacious

cards.front: A tissue is contracting maximally to a saturating dose of a full agonist. You add rising concentrations of a partial agonist (maximum 30% alone) at the same receptor. What happens to the contraction, and why?
cards.back: It falls toward 30%. Each receptor the partial agonist takes is lost to the full agonist and signals weakly, so the partial agonist acts as an antagonist.
cards.quote: Each receptor the weak key takes is one the strong key has lost, so the partial agonist behaves as an antagonist

cards.front: How can a tissue reach its full response before all of its receptors are occupied?
cards.back: Amplification after the receptor: once enough receptors are occupied to saturate the slowest downstream step, more occupied receptors change nothing measurable.
cards.quote: The reason is amplification after the receptor.
cards.section: The gap between the curves: receptor reserve

cards.front: Receptors a tissue does not need for a full response are spare receptors, together called the {{c1::receptor reserve}}.
cards.back: They are ordinary receptors; the tissue simply has more copies than the pathway can use at once.
cards.quote: The receptors not needed are spare receptors, together the receptor reserve.
cards.section: The gap between the curves: receptor reserve

cards.front: An agonist binds its receptor with Kd = 50 nM (radioligand assay). In intact cells its EC50 is 2 nM. What fraction of receptors is occupied at half-maximal response?
cards.back: Occupancy = 2 / (50 + 2) ≈ 3.8%. Half the maximum response needs fewer than 4% of receptors occupied.
cards.quote: Call p the fraction of receptors occupied when the response is half its maximum.
cards.section: The gap between the curves: receptor reserve

cards.front: Does an EC50 well below the Kd prove that a tissue has a receptor reserve?
cards.back: No. A saturating amplifier puts any agonist's EC50 below its Kd, even a partial agonist with no spare receptors. A reserve is present when the tissue reaches its full maximum with less than full occupancy; an EC50 below Kd for an agonist that reaches that ceiling is evidence for it, and receptor inactivation tests it.
cards.quote: A reserve is present when the tissue reaches its full maximum with less than full receptor occupancy; an EC50 below Kd for an agonist that reaches that ceiling is evidence for it, and the receptor-inactivation experiment below tests it.
cards.section: The gap between the curves: receptor reserve

cards.front: After a treatment, an agonist's EC50 in a tissue doubles, but its Kd measured by radioligand binding is unchanged. What could have changed?
cards.back: Either the number of receptors or something after binding (the amplifier); not the drug's affinity.
cards.why: EC50 mixes Kd, efficacy, receptor number and the amplifier; Kd is binding alone.
cards.quote: If a treatment changes a drug's EC50 and leaves its Kd alone, either the number of receptors or something after binding has changed
cards.section: The gap between the curves: receptor reserve

cards.front: A drug gives a full response when only about 5% of its receptors are occupied. Design an experiment to prove a receptor reserve, and state the result that proves it.
cards.back: Destroy increasing fractions of receptors with an irreversible (covalent) antagonist, wash, run full agonist curves, and count surviving receptors with a radioligand. Proof: the curve shifts right first, and the maximum falls only later.
cards.why: With no reserve, the maximum would fall with the first receptors lost.
cards.quote: A rightward shift first and a lower maximum afterwards is the proof.

cards.front: In a sharp-ceiling model, a tissue's pathway saturates once 5% of the original receptors are occupied. Predict the maximum response after an irreversible antagonist removes 80%, and then 97%, of the receptors.
cards.back: 80% removed: 5% of the original is 25% of the survivors, so full maximum, curve shifted right. 97% removed: only 3% remain, so the maximum falls to 3/5 = 60%.
cards.quote: Even with every survivor occupied, the tissue is short of the number it needs.

cards.front: In a receptor-inactivation experiment with an irreversible antagonist, why test a second agonist that acts through a different receptor?
cards.back: If it keeps its full maximum, the blocker left the downstream pathway undamaged, so the fall in maximum reflects lost receptors.
cards.quote: As a control, a second agonist acting through a different receptor should keep its full maximum

cards.front: How does a competitive antagonist change an agonist's dose–response curve on a log axis?
cards.back: The whole curve slides right, parallel to itself, with the same maximum.
cards.quote: on a log axis the whole curve slides right, parallel to itself.
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: Why does a competitive antagonist leave the agonist's maximum response unchanged?
cards.back: It binds reversibly at the agonist's own site, and a receptor holds one or the other. Enough agonist wins the receptors back.
cards.quote: Add enough agonist and it wins the hooks back, so the maximum is unchanged.
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: For a competitive antagonist B at equilibrium, dose ratio = {{c1::1 + [B]/KB}}.
cards.back: Dose ratio: agonist concentration for a given response with antagonist, divided by that without it.
cards.quote: leaving A × (1 + [B]/KB) = A′
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: Why can two curves for the same agonist, with and without a competitive antagonist, give the antagonist's KB in a tissue whose receptor number and downstream steps are unknown?
cards.back: Equal responses on the monotonic, submaximal part of a curve mean equal occupancy by that agonist, so the amplifier cancels and only binding is left (in the equilibrium, single-receptor model).
cards.quote: Equal responses on the monotonic, submaximal part of a curve mean equal occupancy
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: An agonist's EC50 is 4 nM. With 45 nM of a competitive antagonist it is 40 nM, same maximum. Find KB, and predict the EC50 with 495 nM antagonist.
cards.back: Dose ratio 10, so [B]/KB = 9 and KB = 5 nM. At 495 nM, dose ratio = 1 + 99 = 100, so EC50 = 400 nM.
cards.quote: Then 1000 nM of antagonist should give a dose ratio of 101, an EC50 of 1010 nM.
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: A competitive antagonist is applied at ten times its KB to two tissues with very different receptor reserves, each tested with a different agonist acting at the same receptor. Predict each curve's shift, and why this makes antagonists useful for classifying receptors.
cards.back: Both curves shift right 11-fold (1 + 10), whatever the agonist or tissue. The shift depends only on the antagonist's KB at that receptor, so KB values fingerprint receptor types.
cards.why: Rests on dose ratio = 1 + [B]/KB and on equal response meaning equal occupancy, under the lesson's equilibrium assumptions.
cards.quote: That is why antagonist affinities became the fingerprints that told one receptor type from another
cards.section: Blocking the receptor: the shape of the shift names the blocker

cards.front: A Schild plot for an antagonist is a straight line of slope 1, and its pA2 is 8.0. What is KB, and what dose ratio will 100 nM of the antagonist give?
cards.back: With slope 1, pA2 = −log KB, so KB = 10^−8 M = 10 nM. Dose ratio = 1 + 100/10 = 11.
cards.quote: At that point [B] = KB, so pA2 equals −log KB, but only when the slope is 1
cards.section: Schild's test: is it really competition?

cards.front: A Schild plot of log(dose ratio − 1) against log [B] gives a straight line of slope 0.6. What does that tell you?
cards.back: An assumption of simple competition failed: for example the antagonist had not reached equilibrium, the tissue removed the agonist, the antagonist acted allosterically, or more than one receptor contributed. The KB reading is unsafe.
cards.quote: A slope other than 1 means an assumption failed
cards.section: Schild's test: is it really competition?

cards.front: What is the difference between a surmountable and an insurmountable antagonist?
cards.back: More agonist overcomes a surmountable (competitive) antagonist. More agonist cannot overcome an insurmountable one; its signature is a lower maximum, though an irreversible blocker with a receptor reserve can shift the curve right first, and an insurmountable allosteric blocker's effect varies.
cards.quote: a competitive antagonist, which more agonist does overcome, is surmountable
cards.section: Blockers that more agonist cannot overcome

cards.front: A drug blocks a step in the contraction machinery of a smooth muscle, downstream of the receptor. How does it change an agonist's dose–response curve?
cards.back: The maximum falls, and more agonist cannot restore it. Any shift depends on the step blocked.
cards.quote: Lower maximum; any shift depends on the step blocked
cards.section: Blockers that more agonist cannot overcome

cards.front: How does an irreversible antagonist change an agonist's dose–response curve, with and without a receptor reserve?
cards.back: With a reserve: shift right first, then the maximum falls at higher blocker doses. With none: the maximum falls from the start.
cards.quote: With a reserve, shift right first, then the maximum falls; with none, the maximum falls from the start
cards.section: Blockers that more agonist cannot overcome

cards.front: An unknown blocker lowers the maximum of agonist X's curve on gut muscle, and more X does not help. How could you tell a receptor blocker from one acting after the receptor on the contraction itself?
cards.back: Test agonist Y, which contracts the muscle through a different receptor. If Y keeps its full maximum, the block is at X's receptor; if Y's maximum also falls, the blocker acts downstream.
cards.why: Rests on the control logic of the receptor-inactivation design and on post-receptor blockers lowering the maximum.
cards.quote: A non-competitive antagonist binds somewhere else on the receptor, or acts after it, and stops the receptor from responding.
cards.section: Blockers that more agonist cannot overcome

cards.front: A full agonist's dose–response curve is run in the constant presence of a partial agonist at the same receptor. How does the curve differ from control?
cards.back: Response is raised at low full-agonist doses (the partial agonist's own effect); above the partial agonist's ceiling, competition shifts the curve right, but enough full agonist still reaches the full maximum.
cards.quote: Response raised at low full-agonist doses by the partial agonist's own effect; above the partial agonist's ceiling, competition shifts the curve right, but enough full agonist still reaches the full maximum
cards.section: Blockers that more agonist cannot overcome

cards.front: Three agonists rank A > B > C in potency on tissue 1 and C > B > A on tissue 2. What does that suggest about the receptors, and why?
cards.back: At least two receptor types. One kind of binding pocket should give much the same potency order in every tissue.
cards.why: This reasoning sorted adrenaline's receptors into alpha and beta.
cards.quote: One kind of pocket should give much the same order everywhere, he reasoned.

cards.front: In a simple single-receptor preparation at equilibrium, naloxone, a competitive opioid antagonist, is present at 20 times its KB. By what factor must the morphine concentration rise to produce any given effect of that receptor?
cards.back: Dose ratio = 1 + [naloxone]/KB = 1 + 20 = 21, so morphine must rise 21-fold. Naloxone never touches morphine; it changes how many receptors morphine occupies. Clinical reversal is time-dependent and is not predicted by this equilibrium ratio alone.
cards.quote: In a simple single-receptor preparation at equilibrium, naloxone takes receptors without switching them on and moves morphine's concentration-response curve right by a dose ratio of 1 + [naloxone]/KB.

cards.front: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the opiate receptor. Predict its effect when given alone in a tissue with a large receptor reserve, and when given at a high dose on top of a full agonist.
cards.back: Alone, with a large reserve, it can reach or approach the tissue maximum. On top of a full agonist it takes receptors from it and acts partly as a blocker, pulling the response toward its own ceiling.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: a partial agonist's maximum depends on the tissue's receptor number, and it competes with a full agonist.
cards.quote: Buprenorphine, a partial agonist at the same receptor, has a maximum set by its efficacy and by each tissue's receptor reserve

cards.front: Why can't equal responses to two different agonists in one tissue be read as equal occupancy?
cards.back: Efficacy is part of the amplifier's input, so two agonists at equal response are not at equal occupancy. The rule compares one agonist with itself.
cards.quote: two agonists at equal response are not at equal occupancy

cards.front: Two tissues carry the same receptor. A full agonist has Kd = 100 nM; its EC50 is 100 nM in tissue A and 2 nM in tissue B, with a full maximum in both. Predict what an irreversible antagonist removing half the receptors does in each.
cards.back: Tissue A (response tracks occupancy, no reserve): the maximum falls. Tissue B (EC50 far below Kd with a full maximum, evidence of a reserve): in the sharp-ceiling picture the curve shifts right with the maximum intact (a smoother amplifier lets the maximum sag a little).
cards.why: Rests on the reserve test (EC50 below Kd with a full maximum is evidence, tested by inactivation) and the irreversible-blocker rule.
cards.quote: With no reserve, the maximum would start to fall with the first receptors lost.
